Divert means to deliberately turn something — or someone — away from its original path and send it in a new direction.

Picture a river flowing steadily toward the sea. Now imagine engineers building a channel that forces the water to change course and flow into a reservoir instead. That act of making it change course is diverting it.

This one idea — redirecting something from its original path — runs through every single use of the word.

1. To physically redirect something that is moving

This is the most literal sense. When something is on its way from A to B, and you make it go to C instead, you divert it.

  • "Bad weather forced the pilot to divert the flight to a nearby airport." (The plane was heading to one city; it was sent to another.)
  • "Police diverted traffic away from the accident scene." (Cars were sent along a different route.)
  • "Engineers diverted the river to prevent flooding." (The water's natural path was changed.)

Notice something important: the thing being diverted doesn't just stop — it goes somewhere else. Divert always involves a new destination, not just a pause.

2. To redirect attention, focus, or suspicion

You can divert things that aren't physical either — like a person's attention or suspicion. This means deliberately steering someone's mental focus away from one thing and toward another.

  • "The politician diverted attention from the scandal by announcing a new policy."
  • "She diverted his suspicion by acting completely calm."
  • "The magician diverted the audience's attention while switching the cards."

This is worth distinguishing from a similar word: distract often implies an accidental or unwanted break in focus ("The loud music distracted me"). Divert, on the other hand, almost always implies a deliberate, strategic redirection — someone is purposefully steering the attention elsewhere.

3. To redirect money, resources, or effort

When money, funds, or effort that were meant for one purpose are redirected to a completely different purpose, we say they were diverted.

  • "He was accused of diverting company funds into his personal account."
  • "The government diverted money from healthcare to build roads."
  • "After her promotion, she diverted more of her energy toward leadership."

The first two examples carry a negative, often wrongful tone — "diverting funds" in a business or legal context almost always implies misuse. The third is neutral, simply describing a personal shift in priorities. So pay close attention to context: the same verb can be neutral or accusatory depending on the situation.

4. To entertain or amuse someone

This meaning is older and less common in everyday speech today, but you will still encounter it in literature and more formal writing. To divert someone here means to give their mind a pleasant detour — away from boredom, worry, or routine.

  • "The comedian diverted the crowd with clever stories."
  • "She read novels to divert herself during her long recovery."

This is exactly where the word diversion gets its common meaning of "a fun or relaxing activity" — as in, "Cooking is my favorite diversion." The mind is being temporarily redirected somewhere pleasant. Same core idea, just applied to amusement.
The Thread That Connects All Four Meanings

Look at them together:

  • Redirecting a plane → changing its physical direction
  • Redirecting attention → changing someone's mental focus
  • Redirecting money → changing where resources flow
  • Entertaining someone → giving the mind a pleasant detour

In every case, something that was going in one direction is now going in another. Divert always implies a deliberate change of course. Nothing wanders off by accident — something or someone actively causes the redirection.

Divert almost always needs an object — you divert something or someone. It rarely appears alone.

Common patterns you'll encounter:

  • divert + [a thing] → divert traffic, divert funds, divert a river, divert a flight
  • divert + [someone's attention/suspicion] → divert her attention, divert public suspicion
  • divert + [someone] + from + [something] → divert him from his original plan, divert her from the truth
  • divert + [someone] (to entertain) → divert the children, divert the audience
Words That Are Close — But Not the Same

Redirect is the closest word to divert and the two are often interchangeable. However, redirect is more neutral and clean ("redirect the call"), while divert carries a stronger sense of pulling something away from its intended path — sometimes suggesting effort or even interference.

Deflect means to make something bounce off in a new direction — it's commonly used for criticism or blame ("He deflected the question"). It's more about bouncing something away than steering it somewhere specific.

Distract means to accidentally break someone's focus. Divert is almost always more purposeful and strategic than distract.

Divert = to deliberately turn something (a vehicle, water, money, attention, or a person's mind) away from where it was originally going, and send it somewhere else.

Whether you are reading about a detoured flight, diverted river, misused funds, a magician's trick, or someone reading a novel for pleasure — the verb divert is doing exactly the same job every time: making something change course.
